n4h8c0.text: How does Playwright control the browser?
options: The test code is injected into the page as in Cypress, and the Node process only launches the browser and collects the report, so the DOM is available directly without any protocol
Tests run in a Node process and send commands to the browser over a WebSocket protocol: CDP for Chromium, Playwright's own protocols for Firefox and WebKit
Through an extension installed in the browser
Through a WebDriver server: a separate driver per browser, with commands sent as HTTP requests using the W3C WebDriver protocol
n4h8c0.explanation: The test lives outside the browser and talks to it over a persistent connection. That is why Playwright handles several tabs, contexts and domains easily, but DOM access goes through the protocol, not directly.

9p0vz.text: Which browser engines does Playwright support?
options: Only Chromium
Chromium and Firefox, no WebKit
All browsers via WebDriver
Chromium, Firefox and WebKit
9p0vz.explanation: WebKit is Safari's engine, so Playwright lets you check Safari-like behaviour even on Windows and Linux. But it is not the same Safari that users have on a Mac or iPhone.

rihi38.text: What is the fundamental difference between Playwright and Selenium?
options: Playwright runs inside the page like Cypress, so it has direct DOM access and needs no protocol to control the browser
Selenium is faster because it works without a protocol
There is no difference: Playwright is a wrapper around Selenium
No WebDriver middleman: a direct connection to the browser, built-in auto-waiting, isolated contexts and network interception
rihi38.explanation: Playwright has official clients for JS/TS, Python, Java and .NET. The key difference is the architecture: one persistent connection instead of an HTTP request per command, and built-in waiting instead of manual explicit waits.

1lq50s8.text: Is the built-in @playwright/test runner available in every language?
options: Yes, with a caveat: fixtures, projects and sharding exist in every language, and only the HTML report differs, generated by a separate plugin for Python and Java
No: the full runner with fixtures, projects and sharding is JS/TS only; in other languages Playwright is a library used with pytest, JUnit, NUnit
Yes: @playwright/test with fixtures, projects and sharding is equally available for Python, Java and .NET, only the syntax changes
The runner exists only in JS and Python: pytest-playwright has the same projects, sharding and HTML report, while in Java and .NET Playwright works only as a library
1lq50s8.explanation: That is why questions about fixtures, projects and sharding usually mean the TypeScript/JavaScript version.

zp8q7j.text: Mobile emulation with devices['iPhone 13']: what is it really?
options: Emulation: viewport size, user agent, touch and devicePixelRatio in a desktop engine, not a real device
Launching an iOS simulator
Running on a real iPhone through Playwright's built-in device cloud, so Safari behaviour is reproduced fully, gestures included
Native mobile app testing
zp8q7j.explanation: Emulation catches responsive layout problems well but does not replace testing on real devices: performance, mobile Safari quirks, the keyboard.

oc0pan.text: Which locators does Playwright recommend preferring?
options: CSS style classes
Element indexes via nth() and design system CSS classes, because they do not change when the UI is translated
CSS selectors by class and XPath, because they describe the DOM structure most precisely and do not depend on UI text
User-facing ones: getByRole, getByLabel, getByText, getByTestId
oc0pan.explanation: The priority is what the user sees and interacts with: the role and the accessible name. Such locators survive redesigns and check accessibility along the way.

1srrtzw.text: What is a Locator in Playwright?
options: An array of found elements
A reference to a specific DOM element, found as soon as the locator is created and cached until the end of the test
A lazy description of how to find an element; the lookup runs again every time something is done with it
A Promise that resolves to an element
1srrtzw.explanation: page.locator(...) does not search anything when created. So a locator can be declared once (for example, in a Page Object) and used after any re-render of the page.

16z0df0.text: How does a Locator differ from an ElementHandle?
options: ElementHandle is newer and faster: it caches the node and does not look it up again before an action, which is why the docs recommend it over Locator for stable tests
A Locator looks the element up again before every action and has auto-waiting; an ElementHandle holds a specific node and can go stale, and its use is discouraged
A Locator works only with CSS, an ElementHandle supports all selectors; both have the same auto-waiting, so it is a matter of taste
A Locator works only with CSS, an ElementHandle with XPath
16z0df0.explanation: ElementHandle is the old API. If the page re-renders the node, the handle points to a detached element. A Locator does not have this problem.

xrkrg5.text: The page has three “Delete” buttons. What happens?
options: A strict mode violation error: the locator found several elements
A click on the first button in DOM order: Playwright always takes the first match if there are several
A click on a random button: Playwright picks any match and logs a warning
A click on all three buttons
xrkrg5.explanation: Actions require the locator to point to exactly one element. Narrow it down with filter, a container (row.getByRole(...)) or explicitly with first()/nth() when the order really matters.

12mfpmg.text: How do you click “Delete” in the row with the product “Thermos”?
options: page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' }).nth(2), because Thermos is the third row in the table
page.getByText('Thermos').getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' }), because the button is nested inside the text element with the product name
page.getByRole('row').filter({ hasText: 'Thermos' }).getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete' })
page.getByText('Thermos Delete')
12mfpmg.explanation: filter narrows the set of rows by text, and the nested locator looks for the button only inside the row it found. The nth(2) index breaks as soon as the row order changes.

1j5q6wy.text: Which attribute does getByTestId look for by default?
options: data-cy, as in Cypress; the attribute can only be changed with a separate plugin
id
data-testid, but it can be changed with testIdAttribute in the config
data-test
1j5q6wy.explanation: If the project already uses another attribute, for example data-qa, it is enough to set use: { testIdAttribute: 'data-qa' }.

xxirvv.text: How do you work with an element inside an iframe?
options: With a plain page.locator: Playwright searches all the page's iframes itself if the element is not found in the main document
Through page.frameLocator('#payment') or locator.contentFrame(), then ordinary locators
You can't, iframes are not supported
Only through page.evaluate
xxirvv.explanation: Payment forms often live in the provider's iframe. For example: page.frameLocator('#card-frame').getByLabel('Card number').fill(...).

1gsj0cy.text: Do Playwright CSS locators see elements in the Shadow DOM?
options: Yes, CSS and getBy locators pierce the open Shadow DOM; XPath does not
Only the closed Shadow DOM
Only in Chromium
No: the Shadow DOM is isolated, so neither CSS nor getBy locators see it, and you need XPath with a shadow-root function
1gsj0cy.explanation: So web components in Playwright usually need no workarounds, unlike Cypress, which has a separate includeShadowDom option for this.

dt56qy.text: What does Playwright check before click() (auto-waiting)?
options: Nothing: Playwright clicks the element's coordinates right away, and waiting only applies to assertions, not actions
Only that the element exists in the DOM; Playwright does not check visibility or overlap, the browser does
That all the page's network requests have finished, the DOM has not changed for 500 ms and the load event has fired
The element is attached to the DOM, visible, stable (not animating), receives events (not covered) and enabled
dt56qy.explanation: Until the conditions are met, Playwright waits up to the timeout. { force: true } skips some of the checks and can hide a real bug.

1ok4uz9.text: What is the default timeout of web-first assertions expect(locator)?
options: 5 seconds
No limit
30 seconds
1 second
1ok4uz9.explanation: The assertion timeout is 5 seconds, the whole test timeout 30 seconds. For a single check: expect(locator).toBeVisible({ timeout: 10000 }).

duq2oq.text: The text updates a second after the page loads. Which check is reliable?
options: await page.waitForTimeout(1000), then check textContent
expect(await page.getByTestId('status').textContent()).toBe('Paid')
expect(page.getByTestId('status').innerText()).toBe('Paid')
await expect(page.getByTestId('status')).toHaveText('Paid')
duq2oq.explanation: A web-first assertion retries until the text becomes the expected one. In the second option textContent() is read once, and toBe checks an already finished string without retrying.

1rfy5ww.text: What happens if you forget await before an assertion?
options: The assertion runs synchronously and instantly, and Playwright shows a warning in the report, but the test fails correctly
The check is not awaited: the test can finish earlier and pass even if the element is missing
Playwright adds await to expect automatically, so the test behaves the same and only shows a warning in the console
The test always fails with a syntax error
1rfy5ww.explanation: Web-first assertions are asynchronous. A linter with the no-floating-promises rule saves you from such mistakes, and it is worth enabling in the project.

owi4ps.text: How do you reliably check that a list has 10 products that load asynchronously?
options: await page.waitForTimeout(2000), then count()
expect((await page.getByTestId('product').all()).length).toBe(10)
expect(await page.getByTestId('product').count()).toBe(10)
await expect(page.getByTestId('product')).toHaveCount(10)
owi4ps.explanation: toHaveCount retries. count() and all() return a snapshot of the moment and do not wait for all the elements to appear.

18lu5ia.text: Why is page.waitForTimeout(3000) considered an anti-pattern?
options: Playwright ignores waitForTimeout in CI and headless mode, so the test behaves differently locally and on the build server
It blocks all other workers during the pause because the timer is shared by the process, so parallel tests stand still and the total run time grows
The method does not work in headless mode or in CI, so tests that rely on it fail only on the build server
The test always waits the full time and still does not guarantee readiness; it is better to wait for a condition with a web-first assertion or waitForResponse
18lu5ia.explanation: A fixed wait makes tests either slow or flaky. The docs explicitly advise using it only for debugging.

10avx8u.text: How do you wait for a condition that no built-in assertion checks (for example, a status in the database)?
options: expect.poll(() => getStatus(id)).toBe('completed') or an expect(...).toPass() block
Check it once and add retries to the config
There are no built-in mechanisms: you need your own loop with try/catch and an attempt counter
A while (true) loop with page.waitForTimeout(500) and a status check on every iteration until it matches
10avx8u.explanation: expect.poll repeats the function until the value satisfies the matcher; toPass repeats a whole block of checks. Both have a timeout and intervals.

options: An assertion that does not stop the test when it fails: the checks continue, and the test is marked failed at the end
An assertion with a shorter timeout
An assertion that never fails the test
An assertion that checks only an element's visibility, without text or attributes, with a shorter timeout
63p1ap.explanation: Handy when one page has many independent fields to check and you want to see all the mismatches in one run.

options: A single browser tab with its own navigation history that shares cookies and localStorage with the other tabs of the same browser
Playwright's configuration file with browser, locale and viewport settings for the whole project, created in the root next to package.json
An isolated session inside the browser: its own cookies, localStorage and cache, like a separate incognito profile
A separate browser process with its own profile, so every new context launches the browser again from scratch
6wu6zh.explanation: A context is created in milliseconds, so every test gets its own context, and tests are isolated without restarting the browser.

1dimgah.text: What is the object hierarchy in Playwright?
options: Browser → Page → Context → Frame
Page → Browser → BrowserContext → Frame
BrowserContext → Browser → Page → Frame, because the context is created first and the browser launches inside it
Browser → BrowserContext → Page → Frame
1dimgah.explanation: One browser can have several contexts, each context several pages (tabs), and each page a main frame and nested iframes.

1ty2y7b.text: How do you get the page that opens in a new tab after a click?
options: After the click, call context.pages(), wait with waitForTimeout until the array grows, and take the last element
After the click, take context.pages()[1] without waiting: the new tab appears in the list synchronously
First const pagePromise = context.waitForEvent('page'), then the click, then const newPage = await pagePromise
New tabs are not supported: Playwright works with one page per test, so links with target=_blank have to be opened in the current tab
1ty2y7b.explanation: The wait must start before the action, otherwise the event can happen earlier. For popups from a page there is also page.waitForEvent('popup').

1fmth7f.text: How do you test a chat between two users in one test?
options: Two separate tests exchanging data through a file
Create two contexts with browser.newContext(), each with its own session, and open a page in each
Impossible within one test
Open two tabs in one context with context.newPage(), because each tab has its own cookies
1fmth7f.explanation: Tabs of one context share cookies, so they would be one user. Two contexts are two independent users in one browser.

fvb89b.text: What does page.goto() wait for by default?
options: The load event
The user's first click
It returns right after sending the request
Until the network is completely idle
fvb89b.explanation: The waitUntil option changes this: domcontentloaded, load, networkidle, commit. networkidle is not recommended for checks; it is better to wait for a specific element.

1whzhm8.text: What does Playwright do with alert and confirm dialogs if you don't handle them?
options: The test fails with an “unhandled dialog” error
It clicks OK for alert and Cancel for confirm automatically
It accepts them automatically
It dismisses them automatically
1whzhm8.explanation: To check the text or accept the dialog: page.once('dialog', d => d.accept()), before the action that triggers it.

127fx8e.text: How do you check a file download?
options: Check the operating system's Downloads folder after the click, because Playwright saves files there by default
Through page.route on the file's URL
Downloads are not supported in Playwright
const dl = page.waitForEvent('download'); click; const file = await dl; then file.suggestedFilename() and file.path()
127fx8e.explanation: Uploads work similarly: locator.setInputFiles(path) for a file input.

options: A dependency injection mechanism: the test declares in its arguments what it needs (page, request, its own objects), and the runner prepares it and cleans up after the test
JSON files with test data in a fixtures folder, loaded into the test via import and overwritten after the run
beforeAll and afterAll hooks moved to a separate file, imported automatically into every test and run for all the project's specs at once
Saved screenshots for comparison
1bovj4e.explanation: Unlike Cypress, where a fixture is a data file, in Playwright fixtures are objects with a life cycle: setup, use in the test, teardown.

1fpjd7f.text: What does the line await use(...) do in a fixture?
options: Registers the fixture globally for all files and returns the value immediately, and the code after it runs before the test
Repeats the test with a new value
Passes the value to the test and waits for the test to finish; the code after it is the teardown
Returns the value from the fixture and ends it immediately, and teardown runs only through afterEach
1fpjd7f.explanation: Everything before use is setup, everything after is cleanup. The cleanup runs even when the test failed.

mcr6z.text: When does a fixture that the test did not declare in its arguments run?
options: Once per worker
Before every test in the file, because all fixtures declared in test.extend run automatically
After all tests
Never: fixtures are lazy unless marked { auto: true }
mcr6z.explanation: So expensive fixtures do not slow down tests that do not need them. auto: true is for things that must always run, such as collecting logs.

a6yppm.text: How does a scope: 'worker' fixture differ from a 'test' one?
options: It runs after all tests
worker runs only in one of the workers, so tests in other workers get undefined instead of the value
It is created once per worker process and shared by that worker's tests; 'test' is created anew for every test
There is no difference in lifetime: both are created for every test, and worker only limits the fixture to one process
a6yppm.explanation: Worker fixtures are for expensive resources: a database connection, a test account per worker. Their state is shared by the worker's tests, so you can't mutate it freely.

15n3lgq.text: Why are fixtures often better than beforeEach?
options: beforeEach does not exist in Playwright, so setup can only be described with fixtures and test.extend
beforeEach has no access to page
Fixtures run in parallel with each other and beforeEach sequentially, so fixtures are always faster but do not guarantee the order of setup and teardown
They are reused across files, combine, are lazy and have guaranteed teardown next to the setup
15n3lgq.explanation: beforeEach lives within one file, and setup and cleanup are scattered across hooks. A fixture encapsulates the whole life cycle in one place.

7qqy90.text: Why use test.step() in a test?
options: It skips a step if it already passed in a previous test
It groups actions into named steps visible in the report and the trace
It repeats the step on failure
It runs steps in parallel to speed up long tests, and collects the results after all steps finish
7qqy90.explanation: The report reads like a scenario: “Log in”, “Add a product”, “Pay”. Especially useful in Page Objects and in a BDD approach.

options: Sending a request from the test directly
Going to another page
Setting the base URL
Intercepting the page's requests: replacing the response, changing the request or blocking it
hoh35r.explanation: route.fulfill returns your own response, route.continue lets it through (optionally with changed headers), route.abort kills the request.

5jlxar.text: How do you replace an API response with a 500 error?
options: await page.route('**/api/pay', route => route.fulfill({ status: 500, json: { message: 'Error' } }))
await page.waitForResponse('**/api/pay') and check that the server returned 500, because page.route can't change the response status
await page.request.post('/api/pay', { failOnStatusCode: false }) so that the page gets a 500
await page.route('**/api/pay', route => route.abort('500')), because abort takes the HTTP error status
5jlxar.explanation: The route is registered before the action that triggers the request. Then you check that the UI shows a clear message.

v9lo4g.text: How do you change one field in a real server response?
options: route.continue({ body: { balance: 0 } }) changes the server's response body on the fly
Impossible, only a full replacement
const res = await route.fetch(); const json = await res.json(); json.balance = 0; await route.fulfill({ response: res, json })
route.fulfill({ json: { balance: 0 } }) without a server request: Playwright fills in the other fields from the real response itself
v9lo4g.explanation: route.fetch performs the real request, and fulfill with response keeps the original status and headers while replacing the body.

dhiy8r.text: How do you wait for a specific response after a click and check it?
options: await page.waitForTimeout(2000) after the click, then page.waitForResponse('**/api/orders') so the response has surely arrived before the check
page.route with fulfill
const resPromise = page.waitForResponse('**/api/orders'); click; const res = await resPromise; expect(res.status()).toBe(201)
After the click, call await page.waitForResponse('**/api/orders') and check the response status
dhiy8r.explanation: The wait starts before the action, otherwise the response can arrive before we start waiting, and the test hangs until the timeout.

options: The intercepted page request object passed to page.route for changing headers
A recording of all requests in a HAR
Network settings for the browser: proxy, throttling and headers applied automatically to all of the page's requests in the test
An APIRequestContext for HTTP requests from the test without a browser, for API tests and data setup
v45xtj.explanation: request.get/post/put/delete with the baseURL from the config. The response is checked with expect(res).toBeOK() or res.status().

1tbvl3u.text: Does page.route() intercept requests sent with the request fixture?
options: Yes: page.route applies to all of the test's HTTP requests, the request fixture included, because they go through one context
No: request is a separate HTTP client outside the page
Only if request was created from page
Only GET requests
1tbvl3u.explanation: route works with the browser's requests. At the same time page.request shares cookies with the page's context, which is handy for API actions on behalf of a signed-in user.

options: Records the test's trace in HAR format so it can be opened in Trace Viewer along with DOM snapshots
Answers requests from a recorded HAR file: a quick way to mock many endpoints with real responses
Validates the response schema
Exports all the test's network requests to an Allure report in HAR format so they can be viewed after a failure in CI
1fskuki.explanation: The HAR is recorded once from the real backend, and then the tests run stably without it. The downside: the data goes stale and the HAR has to be refreshed.

options: The user's login and password
The context's cookies and localStorage (and IndexedDB if needed), so new contexts start already signed in
Screenshots and videos of the page, so new contexts can reproduce the state the previous test ended in
The state of test variables
1637zmb.explanation: The file is saved after logging in and passed in use: { storageState: 'auth/user.json' }, so tests open without logging in again.

1lxckwl.text: What is the recommended way to log in once for all tests?
options: Log in through the UI in beforeEach of every file, so each test has a fresh session and does not depend on others
One test file with test.describe.serial
globalSetup is the only supported way
A setup project that logs in and saves storageState, with the main projects depending on it via dependencies
1lxckwl.explanation: A setup project is ordinary tests: traces, fixtures and the report work for them. globalSetup is also possible, but without these benefits.

ql1537.text: How do you run some tests in a file without login when storageState is set in the config?
options: Delete the state file before the test, and Playwright creates an empty context without cookies itself
Call context.clearCookies() in every test
This is only possible in a separate project
test.use({ storageState: { cookies: [], origins: [] } }) in the relevant describe
ql1537.explanation: test.use overrides options for a describe block. The same way you can use another role's state: test.use({ storageState: 'auth/admin.json' }).

cmg5gj.text: Tests change the profile settings of the same user in parallel and are flaky. What do you do?
options: Add retries: 3
Turn off parallelism for the whole project with workers: 1, because parallel tests always conflict
Give each worker its own account: a worker-scoped fixture with its own storageState
Increase the timeouts
cmg5gj.explanation: storageState isolates the browser session, not the data on the server. If tests change server state, they need different users. The worker number is test.info().parallelIndex.

r5bl0d.text: How are tests parallelized by default?
options: Everything runs sequentially in one process
All tests in parallel, even within one file, because fullyParallel is on by default
Files are distributed among worker processes, and tests within a file run sequentially
In parallel only across browsers
r5bl0d.explanation: fullyParallel: true or test.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' }) also parallelize tests within a file, and then they must be fully independent.

lf4ahr.text: Can tests in different workers share a module-level variable?
options: Only in headed mode
No: each worker is a separate process with its own memory
Yes: module variables are shared by all workers, because Playwright runs them in threads of one process
Yes, if it is declared with const
lf4ahr.explanation: Shared state between tests is an anti-pattern. Data is passed through fixtures, files (like storageState) or external storage.

ib1jmx.text: What is sharding, and how do you get a single report?
options: Running the same tests in several browsers at once on one machine; the browsers' reports merge automatically without extra commands
Splitting one long test into steps, each running in a separate worker
--shard=1/4 splits the tests across CI machines; each writes a blob report, and npx playwright merge-reports combines them
Caching browsers and dependencies across CI machines to speed up installation before each test run
ib1jmx.explanation: Workers parallelize on one machine, shards across machines. The two mechanisms combine.

1a287tj.text: What does the flaky status in a Playwright report mean?
options: The test was marked unstable manually with an annotation in the code
The test exceeded the timeout
The test was skipped with test.skip
The test failed but passed on a re-run (retries)
1a287tj.explanation: Flaky tests do not fail the run, but they need investigating: a retry masks the problem. Fortunately, a trace on the first retry shows the failure itself.

wr5wxu.text: What are projects in playwright.config for?
options: Setting a different baseURL for each test file and splitting tests by folder so each project has its own package.json and dependencies
Running the same tests in different configurations: browsers, devices, roles, plus setup projects with dependencies
Grouping Allure reports
Splitting the repository into several npm packages with separate dependencies per browser
wr5wxu.explanation: Typically: setup → chromium, firefox, webkit with dependencies: ['setup']. You can run one project: npx playwright test --project=chromium.

1pm2cu.text: Why the webServer section in the config?
options: It configures a proxy
It sets the address of a cloud Playwright server where browsers run remotely
Playwright starts the app itself before the tests and waits until it is reachable
It turns on network interception
1pm2cu.explanation: Handy locally and in CI: npm run start comes up automatically, and reuseExistingServer lets you use a server that is already running.

ebtuy5.text: Tests are stable locally but flaky in CI. Where do you start?
options: Double all timeouts and turn on retries: 5 so the instability does not block merges
Set retries: 5
Add waitForTimeout before every action, turn on retries: 5 and turn off parallelism, because CI machines are always slower than local ones
Open the failure trace, reproduce in the same Docker image and worker count, check dependence on data, order and resources
ebtuy5.explanation: Common causes in CI: fewer resources and more workers, shared test data, a different window size, dependence on test order.

options: A video of the test run recorded at the browser's frame rate, without network or console
A terminal log of all the test's actions and the duration of each step, printed when running with the --reporter=list flag
A Chrome DevTools plugin
A recording of the test run: every action with a DOM snapshot before and after, network, console and source, so you can “rewind” the test
1uoq70f.explanation: It opens with npx playwright show-trace trace.zip or right from the HTML report. The main tool for investigating failures in CI.

options: Tracing is off until you turn on retries in the CLI
The trace is recorded only during the first re-run of a failed test
The trace is recorded for all tests but kept only for those that passed on the first attempt
The trace is recorded only for the first test in the file
18k96zi.explanation: A compromise between usefulness and speed: passing tests do not pay for recording, and failures get a trace. Works only if retries is above zero.

1andr6m.text: How do you debug a test step by step?
options: npx playwright test --debug or await page.pause() at the right spot; also UI mode with --ui
Only through Trace Viewer after the run: Playwright does not support pauses or breakpoints while a test runs
Only through console.log, because Playwright does not support breakpoints in tests
Through the browser's DevTools without Playwright Inspector: open the console and set breakpoints in the test code
1andr6m.explanation: The Inspector lets you step through actions and pick locators; UI mode shows tests with time travel and re-runs on file changes.

1wrpi90.text: What is npx playwright codegen for?
options: It records actions in the browser and generates test code with the recommended locators, as a starting point or to pick a locator
It generates Page Objects for every page of the site by following links like a crawler
It creates the project config
It compiles TypeScript tests to JavaScript and generates fixture types so the editor suggests page locators
1wrpi90.explanation: The generated code is a draft: it has to be rewritten into the project's structure, given assertions and stripped of extras.

7xc0a5.text: toHaveScreenshot() fails in CI although it passes locally. The most likely cause?
options: The GPU is off in CI, so toHaveScreenshot is impossible in headless and has to be turned off
Baseline screenshots depend on the OS and browser: fonts and rendering differ, so baselines are generated in the same environment as CI
A separate paid service is required
toHaveScreenshot works only in headed mode
7xc0a5.explanation: Playwright adds the platform to the baseline name. The practice is to update baselines with --update-snapshots in the Playwright Docker image, and to mask dynamic parts with the mask option.

p0vqq7.text: What does the `exact: true` option do in `getByRole('button', { name: 'Save', exact: true })`?
options: It looks only for visible buttons, ignoring hidden ones and those outside the viewport
It requires an exact, case-sensitive name match, with no substring search
It checks that a button with this name is the only one on the page and throws if there are several
It turns off auto-waiting
p0vqq7.explanation: By default `name` matches a case-insensitive substring, so `Save` also finds “Save draft”. `exact: true` removes those matches. An alternative is the regex `/^Save$/`.

1uboxtk.text: How do you find a product card that contains a “Buy” button but no “Out of stock” badge?
options: `page.getByTestId('card').filter({ hasText: 'Buy' }).filter({ hasNotText: 'Out of stock' }).getByRole('button')` returns the button, not the card
`page.getByTestId('card').getByRole('button', { name: 'Buy' }).not(page.getByText('Out of stock'))`
`page.getByTestId('card').getByRole('button', { name: 'Buy' }).filter({ hasNot: page.getByText('Out of stock') })` applies the filter to the buttons
`page.getByTestId('card').filter({ has: page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Buy' }), hasNot: page.getByText('Out of stock') })`
1uboxtk.explanation: `filter` with `has` and `hasNot` filters parent elements by their content. The second option returns buttons, not cards.

options: Clicking the first of two elements without the strict check: or turns strict mode off, so the action always runs on the first match
Finding an element when one of two variants may appear, for example a cookie dialog or the home page right away
Setting a fallback selector in case the layout changes
Running the action on both elements in turn: first on the first locator, then on the second
hvtprm.explanation: `a.or(b)` matches elements of either locator. If both are visible, the action fails in strict mode, so assertions often add `.first()`.

19g4fze.text: Why is `locator.first()` risky as the main way around strict mode?
options: It hides ambiguity: the test clicks the wrong element if the order changes
It works only with CSS locators
It does not wait for the element and returns at once, so it fails on slow pages
It turns off assertion retries
19g4fze.explanation: `first()` is legitimate when the order is the requirement. As a way to silence the strict mode error it makes the test fragile: better to narrow the locator with a filter or a container.

ua6bou.text: What does `await page.getByRole('listitem').all()` return right after `goto` if the list is still loading?
options: It throws a strict mode error
It waits until at least one element appears and returns all those found at that moment
It waits for the number of elements to stabilize
An array of the elements in the DOM right now, possibly empty: `all()` does not wait
ua6bou.explanation: `all()`, `count()`, `allTextContents()` capture the state here and now. Wait for the condition first with a web-first assertion such as `toHaveCount`, then iterate.

xw130r.text: How does `getByText('Total')` differ from `getByText('Total', { exact: true })`?
options: Without exact it searches only visible text
exact searches only headings and buttons, while without exact the search covers all the page's text, hidden elements included
exact makes the search case-sensitive, and without exact “Total” and “total” are treated as different
Without exact it also finds “Total amount” and “subtotal”; with exact only an element whose full text is “Total”
xw130r.explanation: Substring search is convenient, but on pages with tables it gives extra matches and strict mode violations.

byi1h0.text: Why is `getByRole` considered better than CSS even for internal admin panels?
options: It runs faster, because the browser searches the accessibility tree without walking the DOM
It needs no await and works synchronously, so tests with getByRole are shorter and have no ordering problems
It ignores the shadow DOM
It is tied to what the user and assistive technologies see, and it catches accessibility problems along the way
byi1h0.explanation: If `getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })` does not find the button, the problem is often in the markup: a div instead of a button, or a missing aria-label. That is a signal for the team, not just for the test.

options: The HTML markup verbatim
The page's pixels with roles in mind: the screenshot is compared only within interactive elements
WCAG colour contrast and font sizes in a YAML report
The structure of the accessibility tree (roles, names, nesting) in a YAML-like format
14a2cqd.explanation: An aria snapshot is more stable than a screenshot or HTML: changing classes or styles doesn't break it, but changing the structure the user sees does. Available since Playwright 1.49.

options: toBeVisible does not wait and checks only the current state, while toBeAttached retries until the element appears
toBeAttached checks that the element is focused and accepts input, while toBeVisible only that it is in the DOM
toBeAttached requires only presence in the DOM; toBeVisible also visibility (a size, not hidden)
toBeAttached checks that the element is focused and receives keyboard events
afj67a.explanation: A hidden input or an element with `display:none` passes toBeAttached but not toBeVisible.

1fg2m87.text: Which assertion best checks that a spinner has disappeared?
options: `await page.waitForTimeout(2000)`
`await expect(spinner).toBeHidden()`
`expect(await spinner.isVisible()).toBe(false)`
`await spinner.waitFor()`, which waits for disappearance by default
1fg2m87.explanation: toBeHidden retries and passes if the element is hidden or missing. isVisible captures the state once, and `waitFor()` waits for the visible state by default.

options: toHaveText ignores case and whitespace, while toContainText compares the string character by character
toContainText does not retry and checks the text once, while toHaveText waits for the text to settle for 5 seconds
toHaveText compares the full text (after whitespace normalization), toContainText looks for a substring
toHaveText ignores case and whitespace, so it suits localized texts
dfebfw.explanation: Both retry. With a regex, toHaveText behaves like a pattern search, so `/Total/` passes on “Total: 10”.

options: It changes actionTimeout and navigationTimeout for all actions in the file but does not affect the assertion timeout
It creates a separate expect instance with its own settings, without changing the global one
It turns on soft mode for all assertions with a longer timeout
It changes the whole test's timeout for all the following assertions in the file
r3shxl.explanation: Useful for slow steps: `const slowExpect = expect.configure({ timeout: 10_000 })`. You can also pass a timeout to a single assertion: `toBeVisible({ timeout: 10_000 })`.

options: Repeating a block of several actions and checks until it passes as a whole or the timeout runs out
Running the block in parallel
Skipping the block if it fails and marking the test flaky instead of failed, so it does not block the pipeline
Checking that the function does not throw on the first call, without retries
1h1j5fv.explanation: Unlike expect.poll, the whole block is repeated here: for example, reload the page and check the status. By default the toPass timeout is 0 (no limit except the test timeout), so it is better to set it explicitly.

1fsmayd.text: What is a test's default timeout in Playwright?
options: 5 seconds
30 seconds
No limit
60 seconds
1fsmayd.explanation: The test timeout is 30 s, the expect timeout 5 s; actionTimeout and navigationTimeout are not set by default, so they are bounded by the test timeout.

options: It turns on slowMo for the browser
It marks the test as flaky
It triples the current test's timeout
It slows every action down by 1 second, like slowMo
2g9ucq.explanation: For scenarios that are slow by nature. Don't confuse it with `launchOptions.slowMo`, which slows every action down for debugging.

xr57kp.text: How do you reliably wait for the page change after logging in?
options: `await page.waitForTimeout(3000)`
`await page.waitForNavigation()` after the click, because it is guaranteed to catch any navigation
`await page.waitForURL('**/dashboard')` or `await expect(page).toHaveURL(/dashboard/)`
`await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle')`, because all requests should finish after logging in
xr57kp.explanation: Checking a specific URL or element reflects the intent. The docs advise against networkidle in tests, and `waitForNavigation` is deprecated and prone to races.

1inp776.text: A test checks that there are 0 rows after deleting them. What is more reliable?
options: `expect(await rows.count()).toBe(0)`
`await expect(rows).toHaveCount(0)`
`await expect(rows).not.toBeVisible()`
`await rows.waitFor({ state: 'detached' })`
1inp776.explanation: toHaveCount retries. `not.toBeVisible` on a locator with several elements can behave unexpectedly, and count() captures the state once. The `waitFor` option fails in strict mode if there are several rows.

options: fill sets the value at once and fires input; pressSequentially types character by character with keyboard events
fill does not wait for actionability
pressSequentially clears the field, fill doesn't
pressSequentially clears the field before typing, while fill appends text to what is already there
3zc7h6.explanation: pressSequentially is needed for fields with masks, autocomplete or keydown handlers. The former `type()` is deprecated.

je18qb.text: What does the `{ force: true }` option do in `click()`?
options: It clicks through JavaScript without mouse events
It waits longer: it raises the action timeout to the test timeout so the click works even on slow pages with animations
It skips some actionability checks, so it can click an element a user could not click
It clicks twice in a row so the handler surely fires even if the first click got lost
je18qb.explanation: force masks real bugs: an overlapping modal, a disabled state. Use it only deliberately and with a comment explaining why.

m0agu5.text: How do you choose a file for an `<input type="file">`?
options: Click the input and choose the file in the system dialog with page.keyboard
`await page.getByLabel('Upload').setInputFiles('fixtures/file.pdf')`
`await page.keyboard.type('C:/file.pdf')`
`await page.getByLabel('Upload').fill('fixtures/file.pdf')`
m0agu5.explanation: setInputFiles bypasses the native dialog. If the input is hidden and the file is chosen through a button, `page.waitForEvent('filechooser')` helps.

1ny6zij.text: How do you drag a card to another kanban column?
options: Playwright does not support dragging
`await card.click({ drag: column })`
`await card.dragTo(column)`
`await page.mouse.wheel(card, column)`
1ny6zij.explanation: dragTo does the press, the move and the release. Unusual drag-and-drop libraries sometimes need a manual `mouse.down/move/up` chain.

options: evaluate runs in the Node process
evaluate runs code in the current page right now; addInitScript runs before the page's scripts on every load
addInitScript runs code in the test's Node process, evaluate in the browser after loading
addInitScript works only in the test's Node process, while evaluate runs in the browser after all the page's scripts have loaded
1keml1x.explanation: addInitScript is suitable for replacing `Math.random` or setting a feature flag in localStorage before the app starts. evaluate's arguments must be serializable.

vzw67l.text: How do you run tests with the Polish locale and the Warsaw time zone?
options: `test.use({ locale: 'pl-PL', timezoneId: 'Europe/Warsaw' })` or the same fields in the config's `use`
`page.setLocale('pl-PL')` and `page.setTimezone('Europe/Warsaw')` at the start of each test after goto
Only through the OS settings
`process.env.TZ = 'Europe/Warsaw'` at the start of the test and `page.setLocale('pl-PL')`
vzw67l.explanation: These are context options. Important for fintech: amount and date formats depend on the locale, and the test should pin it explicitly instead of taking it from the CI machine.

19351ta.text: How do you test a “Your session ends in 1 min” banner that appears after 14 minutes of inactivity?
options: Such scenarios can't be automated
Change the CI machine's system time with `process.env.TZ` and `Date.now = () => ...` in Node, because the browser takes the time from the test process
`await page.waitForTimeout(14 * 60_000)` after raising the test timeout with test.setTimeout
With `page.clock`: install the clock and fast-forward time, for example `await page.clock.fastForward('14:00')`
19351ta.explanation: The Clock API (since 1.45) controls Date, timers and setInterval in the page. The test takes seconds, not 14 minutes.
